title: Pork Chops with Cider and Apples
subtitle: Pan-fried pork chops with a cider, apple, and cream sauce
excerpt: Pork chops with cider and apples is a British farmhouse dish: thick pork chops fried until golden, then finished in a sauce of dry cider, sliced apple, and cream. The cider reduces and sharpens, the apple softens and sweetens, and the cream pulls it into a sauce that coats the pork. It is ready in under 30 minutes.
sourceNotes: Pork and apple in cider is a British combination with long roots in West Country and Somerset cooking, where pigs were kept alongside the orchards that produced the cider. The sauce method is related to the Norman dish pork in calvados, filtered through English cider tradition.

content.text: Pork chops with cider and apples is a fast weeknight dish with a sauce that tastes far more involved than it is. Bone-in loin chops work best: they stay juicier than boneless and the bone adds flavour as the chop rests. Use a dry, still cider rather than sparkling; the bubbles dissipate when reducing, but a very sweet cider will make the sauce cloying.

items.prepNote: bone-in loin chops, about 200 g each, at room temperature
Cox, Braeburn, or Granny Smith, cored and sliced

content.text: Season the pork chops on both sides. Heat a frying pan over medium-high heat until hot. Add a little oil and the butter. When foaming, add the chops and cook for 3 to 4 minutes per side until deep golden and almost cooked through. The internal temperature should reach 65°C. Rest on a warm plate for 5 minutes.
In the same pan, cook {{shallot}} sliced shallots over medium heat for 3 minutes. Add the apple slices and cook for 2 minutes until just starting to soften. Add the thyme sprigs.

Pour in {{cider-dry}} of dry cider and bubble for 3 minutes until reduced by half. Stir in {{double-cream}} of double cream and {{dijon-mustard}} of Dijon mustard. Simmer for 2 minutes until glossy. Season and remove the thyme. Return the chops to the pan, spoon the sauce over, and serve.

items.cause: They were cooked too long or the meat was too thin.
items.fix: Bone-in chops at least 2 cm thick stay juicier. Cook to an internal temperature of 65°C for slightly pink pork , safe and tender.

items.cause: A medium or sweet cider was used, or the apple was very sweet.
items.fix: Use a dry cider and a tart apple (Granny Smith or Cox). The Dijon mustard also helps to cut the sweetness.

items.symptom: The apple slices have dissolved into the sauce
items.cause: They were cooked too long before the cider was added.
items.fix: Add the apple after the shallots and cook briefly. The apple should be tender but still hold its shape in the finished sauce.

items.cause: The cream was added to a boiling sauce and not enough liquid remained.
items.fix: Reduce the cider first, then add the cream. Once the cream is in, use a gentle simmer rather than a hard boil.

content.text: Pork and apple in cider is the signature combination of West Country cooking, where pig farming and cider production shared the same landscape for centuries. Somerset and Devon are the heartlands of British cider. A dry, tannic local cider reduces to a sharp sauce that pairs well with the sweetness of pork. The dish travels well beyond its regional roots: it is one of the most reliable weeknight meals in British home cooking.
